title: Messages Down the Wire
sub: Grades 3–4 · Inventions Workshop · The telegraph and Morse code
objective: Students will learn how the electric telegraph worked, part by part: a battery, a key, a wire, a coil and a needle. They will see how Cooke and Wheatstone’s dial and Samuel Morse’s dots and dashes turned letters into signals, send and decode messages in Morse code, and cut a letter down to a telegram — short, because every word cost money.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: The telegraph sent words along a wire as fast as electricity, and changed how people kept in touch. Its codes are the great-grandparents of every text message.

items.question: explain how a key moves a needle miles away?

connection: **Online,** the *Inventions Workshop* lets students build a telegraph, press letters on the five-needle dial, tap Morse code and send a telegram from the telegraph office. **On poster 1,** find the railway, the telegraph and photography among the age’s *iconic innovations*.

steps.title: A message, fast
script: Show the telegraph office. Ask: *“Long ago, before telephones, how could you send a message to a town miles away, fast?”* Take ideas: a rider, a train, a letter. Then, without a word, tap on the desk: short, short, short. *“I just sent you a letter of the alphabet. By the end of today you will be able to read it.”* (It is **S**.)

screen.alt: A painting of a Victorian telegraph office: a long wooden counter with telegraph instruments, pigeonholes of forms on the wall and lamps lit at dusk

steps.purpose: Wonder how a message could travel faster than a person, before any explanation.
students: Long ago, before telephones, how could you send a message to a town miles away, fast?
Listen. Your teacher is sending you a message.

steps.title: Build a telegraph
script: **The circuit.** Go through the five parts on the screen. The **battery** makes an electric current. The **key** is a switch: press it and the current flows; let go and it stops. The **wire** carries the current to a station miles away. There it is wound into a **coil**, and when the current flows through the coil it pushes on a magnet: a **needle**, like a compass needle, which swings for the clerk to read. In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted found that a magnetized needle moved near a wire carrying a current — and moved more if the wire was wound into a coil. If you have a compass, show how its needle swings to a magnet.

screen.caption: Build a telegraph: the five parts, in the order the current reaches them

cells: A switch: press it to send
Wire wound round: pushes on a magnet

steps.purpose: Know the five parts of a telegraph, and follow the current from one to the next.
students: Follow the current: battery, key, wire, coil, needle.
What happens when the key is let go?

steps.title: The needle dial
script: **The dial.** William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone made their five-needle telegraph in 1837. Any two of the five needles swung to point to a letter on a diamond-shaped dial. Ask: *“The dial had 20 letters. C, J, Q, U, X and Z were left off. Why?”* Answer: to save the expense of another needle and its wire. In 1839, the world’s first public telegraph service began, running 13 miles beside the Great Western Railway from London Paddington to West Drayton.

screen.question: The dial had 20 letters. C, J, Q, U, X and Z were left off. Why?

steps.purpose: See how Cooke and Wheatstone made two needles point to a letter, and why some letters were missing.
students: Two needles lean. Where their lines cross is the letter.
What words could you NOT send?

steps.title: Dots and dashes
script: **Morse code.** Samuel Morse’s telegraph used dots and dashes. On 24 May 1844 he sent the message *“What hath God wrought?”* from Washington to Baltimore. Later, needle telegraphs in Britain used Morse code too: the needle leaned left for a dot and right for a dash. Teach the eight letters on the screen; tap them on desks together.

screen.caption: Eight letters to learn first, from the Morse code bench (• dot, — dash)

steps.purpose: Learn a few letters of Morse code, and tap them out together.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three levels build the circuit, decode Morse code and cut a letter down to a telegram.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Match each part to its job; decode a message from a Morse chart; write a word in Morse; cross out words until a telegram fits twelve words.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Put the current’s journey in order; decode two messages and write one; cut a long letter to twelve words; explain why the dial left letters off.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Predict what happens when a part fails; test which words the dial could not send; buy a telegram with a purse of money; explain why the wires ran beside the railway.

steps.purpose: Practice the operator’s skills at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three build the circuit, decode Morse and write a telegram.

steps.title: Decode it together
script: Put the message on the screen and decode it as a class, one letter at a time: **TEA AT TEN**. Then reveal the hook: short, short, short was **S**.

screen.cite: A message from the Morse code bench

steps.purpose: Read a whole message in Morse together, as a clerk would.
students: Decode the message, letter by letter.
Each / is a space between words.

steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back from the screen: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down. Exit question: *“Why did people write telegrams in so few words?”*
